scope: Initial board/source-replay judgements recorded before fresh engine or classifier output. Twenty fixed Black-to-move contexts across five puzzle-source games; omissions are retained. Statements about plausible mechanisms are provisional, not expected labels or ground truth.

cases.judgement: Normal double-fianchetto development. Bg7 does not establish a forcing gain or a tactical f2/f7 attack.
The King's Indian e5 central break leads to ordinary exchanges. Neither the break nor a later bishop pin automatically constitutes a tactical win.
Bg4 attacks Rd1 with tempo but the rook has ordinary retreats. This is not a pin to the king, and any forced gain needs separate evidence.

Bxc5 trades bishop for knight, then Bb7 enables an ordinary rook exchange. The c8 bishop is shielding Ra8 from Rd8; do not confuse that geometry or an equal capture sequence with a won piece. Other defensive resources need engine review.
An eight-piece pawn ending after a knight/pawn exchange. Kf7 centralizes against e5; reserve tempi and a pawn race matter. No zugzwang or promotion headline is proved by the supplied later line.
Kg4 supports a fast h-pawn race. The actual later promotion must not become a promotion action at this king move. Check whether an independently proved root race or exact ending outcome is available.
Black has already lost e5 to the knight. d6 chases it, but retreating is legal; an attack on the knight alone is not a fork or trapped-piece tactic.
b5 seeks queenside space. The supplied later central pawn exchanges and queen trade are not proof of a root tactic.
Bb6 retreats the bishop while retaining a long diagonal. No forced tactical profit is apparent; pressure against e5/f2 and later exchanges need independent verification.
Rxa5 recaptures the bishop that just took Black's bishop on a5. It should not be sold as a fresh hanging bishop. The later Nf2+ fork occurs after further moves and needs its own ply/context.
Nd7 is normal development against a London setup. No immediate tactical mechanism is apparent.
Re8 supports a central break. A later intermediate knight check in the supplied exchanges does not establish a root forcing tactic.
Rxd1+ exchanges equally for the rook that just moved to d1. The king can recapture; giving check is not enough to claim a material tactic.
Kh5 invades toward h4/h3. White can also advance pawns and reposition the rook. Restriction or king activity is not automatically a trap or zugzwang.
Rxd3+ trades rooks into a pawn race. White and Black subsequently queen; inspect exact move order rather than using the captured rook as a material-gain certificate.
Kxh1 recaptures the queen after Qxh1 took Black's queen, reaching bare kings. This is an equal queen liquidation to a draw, not winning a hanging queen.
c6 builds a normal Slav centre. The later bishop trap and mating sequence are unrelated to the immediate development move.
Bh5 retreats the attacked bishop. White's later g4 permits ...Nxg4 and ...Bxh4 mate, but g4 is not forced. Check the defence and mating alternative before attaching any root mechanism.
Black is a gambit pawn up in a King's Gambit. h6 is a pawn/defensive move, not a new material win. There may be sharper alternatives, which need engine analysis.

Nc6 develops, while White can try Ne5 uncovering an attack on its own queen along the g4-d1 bishop ray. The greedy ...Bxd1 branch allows Bxf7+ and Nd5 mate; that branch alone cannot establish a forced root mate or refute every defence to Ne5.
